_link.title: I can explain why each neurochemical can only bind to its corresponding receptor site

toLevel2.stem: What term describes the principle that each neurochemical can only bind to one specific type of receptor site?
distractors: Synaptic compatibility
Neurotransmitter affinity
Chemical permeability

toLevel2.stem: Which analogy is most commonly used to describe the relationship between a neurochemical and its receptor site?
distractors: A bridge over a gap
A plug in a socket
A wave hitting a wall

toLevel2.stem: Why is glutamate unable to bind to GABA receptor sites?
toLevel2.answer: Their molecular structures do not match
distractors: Glutamate is too large to cross the gap
GABA receptors are located on axon sites
Glutamate is released at different times

toLevel2.stem: What determines whether a neurochemical can bind to a particular receptor site?
distractors: Its electrical charge level
Its speed of transmission
Its concentration gradient

toLevel2.stem: According to the principle of receptor specificity, each neurochemical binds to which of the following?
distractors: Any available receptor on site
Multiple receptor types at once
The nearest postsynaptic target

toLevel2.stem: Each neurochemical has a distinct molecular structure that corresponds to only one specific type of receptor site.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A neurochemical can bind to the receptor sites of other neurochemicals if it is present in a high enough concentration.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: The principle that each neurochemical can only bind to one specific type of receptor site is known as {{blank:1}}.

distractors: synaptic transmission
chemical diffusion

toLevel2.stem: A neurochemical cannot bind to a receptor site that does not match its {{blank:1}}.

distractors: electrical potential
concentration level

toLevel2.stem: The relationship between a neurochemical and its receptor site is often described using the {{blank:1}} analogy.

distractors: chain-and-link
wave-and-shore

toLevel3.stem: Which statement best explains the significance of receptor specificity in the nervous system?
toLevel3.answer: It ensures neurochemicals produce specific effects
distractors: It increases the speed of neural transmission
It prevents neurochemicals from being released
It allows neurons to regenerate more quickly

toLevel3.stem: How does receptor specificity explain why neurochemical imbalances affect specific functions rather than all functions equally?
toLevel3.answer: Each neurochemical only activates its own receptors
distractors: Neurochemicals travel to only one brain region
Imbalances are corrected by other neural systems
Each neurochemical is stored in a single neuron

toLevel3.stem: In the lock-and-key analogy for receptor specificity, the 'lock' represents which structure?
toLevel3.answer: The receptor site on the postsynaptic neuron
distractors: The synaptic vesicle in the axon terminal
The ion channel within the synaptic cleft
The dendrite branch of the sending neuron

toLevel3.stem: Maeve learns that glutamate cannot bind to GABA receptor sites. Which concept best accounts for this?
distractors: Glutamate is excitatory and repels GABA
GABA receptors are located on axon sites
Glutamate is reabsorbed before it arrives

toLevel3.stem: Why does receptor specificity mean that different neurochemicals produce different effects on the postsynaptic neuron?
toLevel3.answer: Each receptor type triggers a distinct response
distractors: Each neurochemical has a unique colour code
Receptor sites change shape after each signal
Neurochemicals compete for the same receptor

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following is a direct consequence of receptor specificity?
toLevel3.answer: A neurochemical activates only one receptor type
distractors: A neuron can release only one neurochemical
A receptor site can bind multiple chemicals
A neurochemical is present in one brain area

toLevel3.stem: Receptor specificity explains why a deficiency in one neurochemical affects only the functions associated with that neurochemical rather than all neural functions.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Because of receptor specificity, a deficiency in serotonin would affect only those functions mediated by {{blank:1}} receptors.

distractors: dopamine
glutamate

toLevel3.stem: In the lock-and-key analogy, the neurochemical represents the {{blank:1}} and the receptor site represents the {{blank:2}}.

distractors: lock
door
key
door

toLevel3.stem: Receptor specificity ensures that different neurochemicals produce {{blank:1}} effects on the postsynaptic neuron.

distractors: identical
opposite

toLevel4.stem: Liam is studying a drug that mimics the molecular structure of dopamine. Based on receptor specificity, which receptor sites would this drug most likely bind to?
distractors: All available receptor sites
Serotonin receptor sites only
Both dopamine and GABA sites

toLevel4.stem: A researcher discovers that a patient has fewer serotonin receptor sites than normal. Using the principle of receptor specificity, which outcome is most likely?
toLevel4.answer: Reduced serotonin binding at postsynaptic neurons
distractors: Serotonin binding to dopamine receptor sites
Increased GABA activity at serotonin synapses
Glutamate replacing serotonin at those sites

toLevel4.stem: Aisha reads that a certain toxin blocks glutamate receptor sites. Applying receptor specificity, what would be the most direct effect?
toLevel4.answer: Glutamate cannot bind to its receptors
distractors: GABA cannot bind to its own receptors
All neurotransmitter activity will cease
Glutamate will bind to GABA receptors

toLevel4.stem: Noah learns that a medication increases the number of GABA receptor sites. How would receptor specificity influence the medication's effect?
toLevel4.answer: Only GABA binding would be increased
distractors: All inhibitory chemicals would bind more
Glutamate would also bind to new sites
Dopamine activity would decrease equally

toLevel4.stem: A scientist designs a molecule with the same shape as serotonin. Based on the lock-and-key model, where would this molecule bind?
distractors: At any available receptor site
At dopamine receptor sites
At glutamate receptor sites

toLevel4.stem: Ella observes that a patient with low dopamine levels shows motor difficulties but normal mood. How does receptor specificity help explain this pattern?
distractors: Dopamine is only found in motor regions
Mood is not influenced by neurochemicals
Serotonin compensated for low dopamine

toLevel4.stem: Oliver is told that a new substance has a molecular structure unlike any known neurochemical. Based on receptor specificity, what is the most likely outcome when this substance reaches the synapse?
toLevel4.answer: It would not bind to any receptor site
distractors: It would bind to all available receptors
It would create its own receptor binding
It would mimic the nearest neurochemical

toLevel4.stem: A drug that mimics the molecular structure of a neurochemical can bind to that neurochemical's receptor sites because it matches the {{blank:1}} of the receptor.

distractors: charge
colour

toLevel4.stem: If a toxin blocks GABA receptor sites, receptor specificity predicts that {{blank:1}} would be directly affected while other neurochemicals would {{blank:2}}.

distractors: glutamate binding
dopamine binding
increase in activity
also become blocked

toLevel4.stem: When a medication increases the availability of dopamine in the synapse, only {{blank:1}} receptor sites can be activated because of receptor specificity.

distractors: serotonin
glutamate

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that if enough glutamate is released into the synaptic cleft, it will eventually bind to GABA receptor sites. Which evaluation of this claim is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect, because molecular shape determines binding
distractors: Correct, because high concentration forces binding
Correct, because all neurotransmitters are similar
Incorrect, because glutamate is immediately reabsorbed

toLevel5.stem: Sophie argues that receptor specificity is unnecessary because the nervous system could function equally well if neurochemicals bound to any receptor. Which response best evaluates her argument?
toLevel5.answer: Without specificity, precise neural signalling would fail
distractors: Her argument is valid because binding is random
Specificity only matters for excitatory chemicals
Without specificity, signals would travel much faster

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes that a new drug will treat anxiety by binding to serotonin receptors, but its molecular structure closely resembles dopamine. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: The drug would likely bind to dopamine receptors instead
distractors: The drug would bind to serotonin receptors as intended
The drug would bind to both receptor types at once
The drug would not bind to any receptor type at all

toLevel5.stem: Marcus states that receptor specificity means a neuron can only receive one type of neurochemical. Which evaluation of this statement is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; a neuron can have multiple receptor types
distractors: Correct; each neuron has only one receptor kind
Correct; neurons are specialised for one chemical
Incorrect; neurons do not have receptor specificity

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that the lock-and-key analogy is misleading because real locks can be picked with different keys. Which response best evaluates this critique?
toLevel5.answer: The analogy highlights shape-matching, not security
distractors: The critique is valid and the analogy should not be used
The analogy is perfect and has no real limitations
Lock-picking parallels neurochemical concentration levels

toLevel5.stem: Dr Chen claims that receptor specificity is the primary reason why a serotonin deficiency affects mood regulation but not motor control. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Supported, as serotonin binds only to its receptors
distractors: Unsupported, because all neurochemicals affect mood
Supported, because serotonin is found only in one area
Unsupported, because motor control also uses serotonin

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that receptor specificity makes the nervous system inefficient because each neurochemical requires its own receptor type. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Specificity enables precise control of neural functions
distractors: The student is correct that specificity is wasteful
Efficiency is unrelated to receptor binding processes
A universal receptor would improve neural processing

toLevel5.stem: Isla claims that if a drug has a similar but not identical molecular structure to dopamine, it could still partially activate dopamine receptors. Which evaluation best applies the lock-and-key model?
toLevel5.answer: Possible, as a close shape match may allow partial binding
distractors: Impossible, because only exact matches allow any binding
Guaranteed, because all similar molecules bind the same
Irrelevant, because drugs cannot interact with receptors

toLevel5.stem: A claim that increasing glutamate concentration would cause it to bind to GABA receptors is {{blank:1}} because receptor specificity depends on molecular {{blank:2}}, not concentration.

distractors: correct
plausible
quantity
velocity

toLevel5.stem: The lock-and-key analogy is useful for explaining receptor specificity because it emphasises that binding depends on the {{blank:1}} between the neurochemical and the receptor site.

distractors: charge match
speed match
